passage:
At the Monday meeting in the small branch office above the fertiliser shop, Gautam Sir read out the collection figures and clapped for Mahesh. 'No excuses, no questions. That's how you get to district level.'
Jaya kept her eyes on her register. Two months ago she had asked, politely, whether the evening visits to borrowers' homes were becoming too harsh. The next week she was moved to the far villages with the worst roads and the smallest targets, and she stopped being invited to tea with the team.
Now Mahesh caught her eye and grinned. The team had covered for her when her mother was ill. She owed them.
Her father's pension didn't stretch far. This job did.
When Gautam Sir asked, 'Any concerns?', Jaya said nothing, and hated how easy it was.

qa.q: Where was Jaya moved after she asked her question?
qa.a: She was moved to the far villages with the worst roads and the smallest targets.

qa.q: Why does Jaya stay silent when Gautam Sir asks for concerns?
qa.a: She fears losing a job her family relies on and feels she owes the team, so loyalty and fear outweigh her unease, which she hates.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Jaya at this stage?
qa.a: She could write down what she has seen and find one trusted colleague or an official channel to raise the harsh visits, so she is not carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might the borrowers be affected by a team where no one questions the visits?
qa.a: They may face growing pressure at home in the evenings with nobody inside the branch willing to speak up for fair treatment.

grounding: It shows a manager praising unquestioning results and sidelining a worker who raised a concern, so loyalty and job fear keep her silent.

In the site office in Johannesburg, the whiteboard had a new column: 'Delivered - no drama'. Omar, the project manager, added a gold star beside Zanele's name for finishing the third floor early.
'This is what I like,' he told the team. 'People who get it done and don't bring me problems.'
Nobody mentioned Thabo, who had asked last month why the concrete tests were being signed before the results came back. Thabo now did night inventory in the yard.
Zanele looked at her gold star and felt her stomach tighten. She had noticed the same thing as Thabo. She had said nothing.
Her younger brother's university fees were due in March. And the crew had been good to her, sharing lunch, covering her first mistakes.
She smiled for the photo Omar took of the board.

qa.q: What did Omar add beside Zanele's name?
qa.a: He added a gold star for finishing the third floor early.

qa.q: Why does Zanele's stomach tighten as she looks at her gold star?
qa.a: She knows she noticed the same problem as Thabo and stayed quiet, so the reward feels wrong even as fear and loyalty keep her silent.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Zanele at this stage?
qa.a: She could quietly talk to Thabo, note what she has seen, and look for a proper channel such as a safety officer to raise the concrete tests.

qa.q: What might Thabo be experiencing on night inventory?
qa.a: Thabo is likely feeling punished and isolated for asking an honest question while quieter colleagues are praised.

grounding: It shows a manager rewarding results without questions and sidelining the one who asked, while a young engineer stays silent out of fear and loyalty.

At the Monday review in the bank branch in Lucknow, Mehak, the branch manager, wrote two names on the whiteboard under Stars: the officers who had sold the most insurance with every loan. Nobody asked how. Everyone knew some customers didn't understand what they had signed.
Hansa's name wasn't there. Last month she had asked, in this same meeting, whether elderly customers should have the policy terms read aloud. Mehak had smiled and said, "Hansa, let's keep the focus on targets." Since then Hansa had been moved from the big accounts to the counter, and left off the team lunch.
Now, looking at the stars, she felt the familiar tightness in her chest. She had rent. Her father's medicines. And the team had been kind to her when she joined.
When Mehak asked, "Any concerns before we close?", Hansa looked down at her notebook and said nothing. Nobody else did either.

qa.q: What were the officers under Stars known for?
qa.a: They had sold the most insurance with every loan.

qa.q: What did Hansa feel when Mehak asked for concerns?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid for her job, and torn by loyalty to the team, so she stayed silent.

qa.q: What could Hansa do outside that meeting?
qa.a: Note her concern in writing and take it to a proper channel, such as the bank's compliance or ethics office, rather than carry it alone.

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to see concerns raised in meetings?
qa.a: Mehak treats them as distractions from targets and quietly sidelines those who raise them.

grounding: A manager rewards results without questions and sidelines a young officer who raised a concern, and fear and loyalty keep her silent.

passage:
Dear Urmila,
Remember how you used to call me the class conscience? I don't think you would now.
At the construction firm we have a monthly safety checklist. For three months I've watched the site head sign it without walking the site. In January I said so in a meeting. Nothing happened, except that I stopped being invited to planning calls and my appraisal said I'm "not a team player".
Kiran, who laughed along and signed whatever was put in front of her, has just been promoted.
So now I keep my mouth shut. The team has been good to me in other ways, and I can't lose this job, not with my mother's surgery coming. The one thing I still do is walk the scaffolding myself every Friday and get the foreman to fix what I find.
I hate how quiet I've become. Tell me I'm not a coward.
Lavanya

qa.q: What does the site head do with the safety checklist?
qa.a: Sign it without walking the site.

qa.q: What does Lavanya feel about having gone so quiet?
qa.a: Lavanya feels ashamed and afraid, silenced by fear for the job and by being sidelined after speaking up.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do beyond the Friday walk?
qa.a: Write down what has been seen and take it in writing to the firm's safety or ethics office, perhaps with Urmila's support.

qa.q: What might Urmila feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Urmila would likely feel sad and protective, and want to remind Lavanya that the conscience is still there.

grounding: A young engineer is sidelined for raising a concern while those who go along are rewarded, and fear for the job keeps the writer quiet.

Zubin, you asked why I don't just say something. Let me explain how it works.
Every month our team inflates the campaign numbers for clients. Buys a few thousand fake views, rounds up the reach. Our boss calls the people who deliver "my rockstars". The last person who asked if this was okay, a quiet designer called Leena, was taken off every big account within a month. Now she does brochures in the corner.
And our team lead, Ashok, is the one who trained me, got me this job, and covered for me when my father was in hospital. If I raise it, I'm raising it against him.
So I stay quiet. I tell myself I'm being loyal. But at night I feel as if I've swallowed a stone. I'm Harish, and I'm scared, and I hate that I'm scared.

qa.q: What happened to Leena after she asked?
qa.a: She was taken off every big account within a month.

qa.q: What does Harish feel at night?
qa.a: Harish feels anxious and heavy, like having swallowed a stone, caught between loyalty to Ashok and unease.

qa.q: What could Harish do with this unease?
qa.a: Talk it through with someone trusted, keep a private record, and look for a proper channel to raise it rather than act alone.

qa.q: How might Leena feel doing brochures in the corner?
qa.a: Leena likely feels sidelined and hurt, punished for asking an honest question.

grounding: A young employee sees a questioner sidelined and results rewarded, and loyalty to a mentor and fear keep the speaker silent.

First week of March: at the sales review, Rashmi asked the regional head why customers were being told the loan offer had "no hidden charges" when the processing fee was in the fine print. The room went quiet. Maria, sitting beside her, looked at her notebook.
Two weeks later: the monthly awards were announced. Top performer went to the man who closed the most loans, no questions asked. Rashmi had been moved off the big corporate accounts "for fresh perspective." Everyone understood.
End of April: in a team huddle, a trainee asked Maria, quietly, if the fee line was really okay. Maria felt her throat tighten. She thought of her rent, her younger brother's college fees, the team that had welcomed her. "Just follow the script," she said. That night, she lay awake a long time, the trainee's face in her head.

qa.q: What was Rashmi moved off, and for what stated reason?
qa.a: Rashmi had been moved off the big corporate accounts for fresh perspective.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the trainee asked about the fee line?
qa.a: Maria felt anxious and torn, afraid for her job and her family's needs and loyal to her team, yet uneasy enough to lie awake afterwards.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Maria at this stage?
qa.a: Maria could note down what she has seen and talk to someone she trusts outside the sales chain, such as the compliance team, instead of repeating follow the script.

qa.q: How might the trainee feel after Maria's answer?
qa.a: The trainee may feel confused and let down, learning from someone they trusted that questions are not welcome here.

grounding: Shows managers rewarding results without questions and sidelining a colleague who raised a concern, while fear and team loyalty silence someone still uneasy.
